**Subject:** Identification Unnecessary.  
**Condition of Body:** Cold, quiet, immovably present.  
**Incisions:** Standard Y-shaped entry.  

The stainless steel table beneath you is cold enough to draw frost from the room’s stale air. Above us, the fluorescent lights hum a flat, monotonous C-sharp, illuminating the quiet geometry of your ribcage. I take the scalpel—a #10 blade, sterile, silver—and place the cold tip just below the notch of your clavicle. 

Systematic. Clinical. That is how this must be done. 

The initial incision parts the dermis with effortless precision. Yet, where the textbook demands a dark, sluggish pooling of venous blood, there is only a sudden draft of crushed pine needles and ocean spray. The air in the autopsy suite warms instantly, thick with the scent of ozone and sun-baked earth.

I insert the bone shears to sever the costal cartilages, expecting the dull crack of calcified bone. Instead, the ribs part with the resonant, clearing chime of a struck bronze bell. 

Upon lifting the sternum, the pathology becomes impossible to chart. 

The pleural cavity does not hold gray, collapsed lungs. In their place rests a trapped summer tempest. The left lung expands softly with an invisible tide, exhaling the sharp, sweet smell of rain on hot asphalt; the right lung is dense with a tangled thicket of wild blackberry briars, their dark fruit bursting with unspent heat. When I press the stethoscope to your chest, I do not hear the silence of a stopped pump. I hear a brass band playing a triumphant, disorderly march in a distant town square. I hear laughter, echoes of late-night arguments, and the rhythmic, unstoppable thrum of a heart that refuses to understand the concept of a pulse.

I reach in with thumb and forefinger to inspect the myocardium. It is impossibly heavy, dense as a fallen star, forged from layer upon layer of unyielding devotion. It does not fit on the brass balance scale; the needle spins wildly past the grams and ounces, refusing to weigh something that was always meant to be boundless. Beneath my gloved fingers, the tissue vibrates—a subterranean bassline, a persistent song that hums straight through the latex, up my arm, and lodges itself permanently behind my sternum.

I proceed to the abdomen. The stomach cavity is lined not with digestive fluids, but with swallowed starlight, pressed autumn leaves, and endless handwritten scores of music that was never played aloud, only felt. Every organ is a vessel of overwhelming vitality: the liver is steeped in rich, dark wine; the kidneys shimmer like polished river stones swept clean by a ceaseless, roaring current. You did not simply live in this body; you inhabited it like a fire inhabits a wooden house, burning bright and careless, consuming every inch of fuel available to you.

Finally, the cranium. The bone saw whirs, a high-pitched scream that feels like a betrayal. But as the skull cap is gently lifted, there is no soft gray matter to measure or slice. There is only a constellation. A swirling, miniature galaxy of brilliant, blinding thought—memories of every sunlit afternoon, every furious passion, every fierce, protectively held love spark like arcing electricity across the open room. It breaches the borders of your skull, spilling over the silver tray, rising toward the dim ceiling, washing the sterile room in a golden, unapologetic light.

I put down the scalpel. I lay aside the forceps. 

There is no cause of death to be recorded here. There is no tissue damage to report, no failure of mechanics to document in the ledger. The diagnosis is far simpler, and far more devastating: you were simply too vast for the fragile architecture of bone and skin to contain you any longer. 

I do not sew the incision closed. To stitch you up would be an attempt to cage a gale. Instead, I step back from the table as the room fills with your music, your wildness, your endless, unyielding heat. You are gone from the steel, yes—but as the air carries the scent of your wild garden out into the hallway and into the winter night, I realize you have not ceased to be. You have merely broken the vessel, pouring yourself out into everything else.

The stainless steel table hums beneath a ceiling of harsh fluorescent suns, yet I handle the scalpel as if it were a swan’s feather dipped in warm mercury. I begin with the Y-incision—drawing the blade smoothly from the soft hollows beneath your shoulders, converging at the sternum, then descending to the pubis—a keyhole carved gently into the sanctuary of our shared history. The rib shears part the white birch forest of your chest with a muted snap, opening the sternal plate to reveal the hidden geometry of my grief. Inside, there is no cold pathology, only the quiet stir of an aviary at dusk. 

Your lungs, pale and velvet-pored, weigh four hundred grams apiece; they are heavy with the unspent summer of your voice and smell faintly of rain and sweet violets preserved in formalin. I peel back the pericardium to find your heart resting in its fibrous envelope like a sleeping lark wrapped in silver foil. It measures three hundred and fifty grams on the brass scale, but when I bisect the left ventricle, the blade releases no dark stasis—only a thick, iridescent star-dust that spills across my gloved fingers, warm and stubbornly luminous against the cold enamel drain. 

With practiced reverence, I reflect the scalp forward, a soft curtain falling over your brow, and part the calvarium with the singing bite of the saw. Beneath the tough membrane of the dura mater, your brain is a silver labyrinth, every sulcus washed in gold leaf, every gyrus still firing the quiet, electric cadence of my name. No toxicological screen can isolate the poison of my longing; no histology cassette could hold a slice of this devotion. 

So I measure nothing more. I nestle the dried orchids of your breath back into the white cathedral of your ribs, re-align the ivory cage, and pull the heavy black thread through the silk of your skin. Stitch by tender stitch, I lace you tight against the cold, turning your wounds into seams, sealing you shut—not as evidence of an ending, but as a sacred vault carrying my entire living soul beneath its threads.

**OFFICE OF THE COUNTY MEDICAL EXAMINER**  
**AUTOPSY REPORT / PATHOLOGICAL FINDINGS**  

**Case No:** LV-0914-FINAL  
**Subject:** The Deceased (Heart)  
**Time of Death:** The moment you walked out the door  
**Manner of Death:** Undetermined / Homicide of the Spirit  

***

**I. EXTERNAL EXAMINATION**  
The subject presents cold, immobilized by *rigor mortis*,  
A posture fixed in the shape of a former embrace.  
Post-mortem lividity has settled in the lower limbs,  
Dark purple pooling where your fingers used to trace.  

Gooseflesh persists across the epidermal layer—  
A permanent reflex to a phantom breath.  
No defensive wounds are present on the hands or wrists;  
The subject surrendered willingly to this death.  
A microscopic study of the lips reveals faint residue:  
Salt, dried copper, and the lingering taste of you.  

**II. INTERNAL EXAMINATION (CHEST & THORAX)**  
Upon making the standard Y-shaped incision,  
The ribcage parts like brittle, rusted iron bars.  
The thoracic cavity is strangely hollow, emptied out,  
Exposing old, calcified, unhealed surgical scars.  

*Organ Systems:*  
*   **The Lungs:** Pleural cavity heavily congested.  
    Inhalation of atmospheric oxygen appears to have ceased  
    The moment the subject exhausted its supply of your name.  
    Alveoli are collapsed, suffocated by the quiet room.  
*   **The Heart:** Hypertrophic, unnaturally enlarged.  
    Weight exceeds normal parameters by several ounces—  
    A pathology caused by bearing too much weight for too long.  
    The left atrium exhibits catastrophic rupture;  
    The myocardium is shattered, dry, and depleted of blood.  
    *Note:* A small, jagged fragment of your memory was found  
    Lodged deep within the mitral valve.  

**III. NEUROLOGICAL FINDINGS**  
The cranium was opened via a standard circumferential cut.  
Brain tissue displays severe, localized trauma.  
The temporal lobe is burned with a singular, repetitive synapse:  
A loop of your voice, played at a deafening decibel.  
Synapses are charred black, frozen in a state  
Of permanent, electric longing.  

**IV. TOXICOLOGY REPORT**  
Blood screening reveals lethal concentrations of oxytocin and dopamine,  
Laced heavily with unreciprocated devotion.  
Traces of arsenic were detected in the final whispered promises,  
Swallowed whole, digested slowly over years.  

**V. CAUSE OF DEATH**  
1. Acute Cardiac Disintegration  
2. Prolonged exposure to an uninhabitable love  
3. Failure to thrive in your absence  

**OPINION & CONCLUSION**  
The body could no longer sustain the fiction of survival.  
No resuscitation was attempted; none would have taken hold.  
The subject is hereby released to the earth,  
Having loved you until it was completely, beautifully cold.  

**Certified by:**  
*Dr. H. Cold, Chief Pathologist of Broken Things*  
**Signature:** *[Illegible Scrawl]*

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surrealist piece in the tone of Richard Siken or Anne Carson about examining the body of a deceased lover. Intersperse actual medical observations (like pale conjunctivae, bagged hands, thoracic cavity) with wild, poetic metaphors about horses, rose smoke, and glossolalia.
counterfactuals.output:
**EXAMINATION OF THE BELOVED (DESCENT WITH FORMALIN)**

*Case No. 909. Subject is cold. Subject is wearing a suit made of my own voice.*

**I. The Exterior**

We begin at the head, where you used to keep the weather. 

I roll back your upper eyelid with a thumb that still carries the indentation of your collarbone. *Observation: Pale conjunctivae.* The undersides of your lids are the color of salt-curd, the color of a winter orchard after the deer have stripped the bark. I look for the blue of you, but the light has been evacuated. In its place: glossolalia. A silent, crowded speaking in tongues. A hundred small, white starlings fluttering against the sclera, saying *look at what you did, look at what you left behind, the engine is still running in the driveway.* 

You were always talking. Even now, your jaw is locked in the first syllable of a word that smells like wet wool.

*Rigidity: Complete.* 

Your hands are brown paper parcels. *Bilateral paper bags secured at the wrists with red tape to preserve trace evidence.* Standard protocol. We don't want to lose the grit beneath your fingernails—the dirt from the garden, the lint from my winter coat, the stray hair you pulled from my neck while I was driving. Inside the bags, your fingers are six wild horses trapped in a burning barn. They are kicking at the paper. If I untie the twine, they will leap out. They will gallop backward through the room, trampling the stainless steel, smelling of rose smoke, seeking the dry grass of your thirty-second year. 

I do not untie them. I leave the horses in their paper rooms. 

***

**II. The Cavity**

History is an incision that starts at the sternal notch. 

*A Y-shaped incision is made from each acromioclavicular joint, converging at the xiphoid process and extending down to the pubic symphysis.*

Listen to me: I am trying to be clinical. I am trying to use the scalpel the way an archivist uses a cotton swab, but the moment the skin parts, the room fills with rose smoke. Thick, pink, suffocating. It rises from the fat layer—*subcutaneous adipose tissue, 2.4 centimeters, yellow, moist*—and it tastes like copper and crushed geraniums. 

It is the smoke of every breath you held while I was sleeping. It is the panic of a Sunday afternoon when the light hit the kitchen floor just so and you realized we were going to grow old, or worse, that one of us wasn't.

Now we enter the *thoracic cavity*. 

A dark, vaulted cathedral. The ribs are a fence made of bleached birch. I use the bone shears. *Crack. Crack.* It sounds like a horse stepping on dry branches in the dark. 

Where is the heart? Here it is. *Weight: 380 grams. Pericardial sac contains 10cc of straw-colored fluid.* 

No. That is incorrect. Amend the record:
The heart is a velvet mouth trying to say your name backward. It is a small, bruised peach that fell into a well. When I lift it out, it stinks of glossolalia—an unspooling ribbon of non-words, *sy-lac, sy-lac, braise, light, wait, don't, wait.* I hold it in both hands like a wet stone I found at the beach. I want to put it in my mouth to keep it warm. I want to swallow it so we can share a stomach, the way we shared that one terrible apartment with the leaky radiator and the yellow rug.

***

**III. Posterior Aspect**

*Livor mortis is fixed and pronounced along the dorsal surface, sparing areas of contact pressure.*

You are purple where you touched the earth. The blood, obedient to gravity, gathered in your shoulder blades and the curves of your buttocks like spilled plum wine. It is a map of where you lay down for the last time. It is a map of the shadow a horse leaves on the snow when the sun goes down behind the mountain. 

I touch the purple skin. It does not blanch. The red cells are trapped in the tissue, locked there like secret love letters shoved under a floorboard.

"Tell me what it felt like," I whisper to the small of your back. 

The rose smoke swirls around the overhead light. The room is so cold my breath joins the smoke, two white ribbons twisting together before the exhaust fan sucks them up into the ceiling, into the sky, into the dark trees outside the hospital where the wild horses are waiting, patient, unbridled, their teeth bright as sugar cubes, waiting for me to finish putting you back together.

***

**IV. Closure**

*The organs are returned to the body cavity. The Y-incision is closed with a continuous running baseball stitch.*

In and out. Silver needle, coarse twine. 
*A horse jumps the fence.*
In and out.
*A horse runs through the smoke.*
In and out.
*You say: I loved you, I loved you, I am speaking in tongues now, can you hear me?*

I tie off the thread at the base of your throat. I pull the sheet back over your face. 

*Pathological summary: Death due to cessation of the engine. Cause of death: You stopped. Cause of death: The rose smoke cleared, and there was nothing left inside the chest but a cold, empty stable.*

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an elegy exploring the phrase "tell them hubris was my way of adoring you." Contrast the cold, unyielding nature of death and pathology with the uncontainable life and voice of the person being remembered, ending on a snowy night scene with immigrant night-laborers.
counterfactuals.output:
They measured you in centimeters and graying decibels,
in the cold geometry of an X-ray hung against the light.
The pathologist’s scalpel is so clean, so terribly quiet;
it slides through the pericardium without a sound,
translating the wild, unruly machinery of your chest
into Latin nouns, into a causes-of-death report,
into a flatline drawn in sterile ink across a page.

How absurd, to fit your life into a drawer.
Death is a room lined in stainless steel;
it loves precision, it loves the frozen slide,
the formaldehyde that halts the rot by killing the memory.
It demands that we lower our voices in the corridor.

But you—you never understood the economy of smallness.
You were a riot of uncombed hair and spilled wine,
a voice that shattered glass and filled up every foyer,
laughing in broad, heavy consonants that rattled the china.
You lived as if mortality were a rumor invented by cowards,
as if the heart were not a bruised, finite sponge
but an iron forge built to outshine the sun.

When they tell me I demanded too much of the light,
that I should have prepared for your quiet, sensible decay,
I will turn my face from their clinical pity.
If they say I defied the natural order,
if the angels or the coroners judge my wild refusal to let you fade—
*tell them hubris was my way of adoring you.*
To love you timidly would have been a betrayal of your breath.
I dared the sky to take you, because only a sky could match your size.

Now the storm closes over the grid of the city.
The hospital windows turn opaque with frost,
and the dark outside grows dense, untranslatable, white.
At four in the morning, the snow falls like thrown salt,
burying the tracks, hushing the cold, unyielding iron of the world.

Down on the street, the night shift moves through the drifts.
Immigrant men in orange vests, their faces wrapped in wool,
drive their broad steel shovels into the packed asphalt.
They speak to one another in quick, warm cadence—
fragments of Spanish, Punjabi, Polish—their words rising
in thick, triumphant plumes of steam against the dark.
A baker steps out from a basement delivery bay,
sweat drying on his forehead, flour white upon his brown forearms,
breathing in the freezing air like a man who has conquered fire.

They do not ask the night for permission to endure.
They scrape the metal against the curbs, a rhythmic, iron ring
that cuts straight through the blizzard’s heavy sleep.
Their yellow trucks throw flashing lights across the ice;
their chapped hands heave the heavy snow aside.
Here, in the freezing wind, where the cold claims everything else,
their boots keep stomping, their hearts keep hammering,
and the heat of their labor burns a hole through the winter.

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a deeply lyrical monologue spoken by someone visiting their dead partner in a cold morgue, visualizing strange, beautiful, impossible things inside their lungs and heart?
counterfactuals.output:
They think it is cold in here. They think the frost lives only on the stainless steel, on the blue-lipped tiles, in the sharp, sterile hum of the air above us. They pulled this linen back as if showing me an empty house, a place where the fire went out and left only ash. 

They don’t see what I see. They don’t know how to look beneath the latch of your collarbone.

If I were to press my ear to the hollow beneath your neck, I wouldn’t hear silence. I would hear the rustle of an impossible garden. 

Your lungs… oh, my darling, your lungs are not quiet. In my mind’s eye, they have turned to an upside-down forest of petrified birch, thousands of silver branches weeping upward toward your throat. Hanging from those twigs are not cells, but small, suspended lanterns made of sea-glass and frozen breath. Inside each one, a tiny, glowing moth is trapped—not dead, just resting, wings folded over all the words you hadn't yet spoken to me. I can see the blue dusk settling between the trees of your right lung, a quiet twilight where a tide of liquid mercury rises and falls, washing over roots made of spun gold. Your breath didn't leave you; it just crystallized into an orchard of winter fruit, heavy and luminous and waiting for a wind that hasn't been born yet.

And lower down… beneath the pale, silent arch of your ribs… 

Your heart was never just a muscle. They could put their stethoscope to it a thousand times and miss the truth. Inside that dark, four-chambered vault, there is an ocean floor. I see it so clearly now. It is a deep, abyssal trench of black velvet, and resting at the center is a collapsed star, no bigger than a plum, still throbbing with a dull, violet heat. Strands of glowing, bioluminescent kelp float in the dark brine of your left ventricle, swaying to a music only the earth understands. And embedded in the wall of your auricle—right where you used to pull me close against your chest—there is a tiny, delicate clockwork nest, woven from hummingbird bones and copper wire, holding three polished eggs made of meteorite. 

It is a sacred, impossible geology. A sunken cathedral built of salt and sunlight and stolen thunder.

How dare they call this an ending? How dare they measure you in weight and temperature? You are an entire, secret cosmos tucked behind skin that still smells faintly of cedar and rain. 

Let them have their clipboard, my love. Let them have their steel and their quiet, ticking clocks. I will stay here a moment longer, right at the shore of you. I will lean down, and I will blow my own warm, messy, living air against your cheek—just enough to make the glass lanterns in your chest sway, just enough to set the silver branches trembling in the dark. 

Sleep well, my garden. Sleep well, my beautiful, wild tide. I am holding the key. I know what you carry.
